fixes.explanation: Nobody there says stay home. The prophets tell Ahab, “Go up,” and “…the Lord will deliver it into the hand of the king.” (1 Kings 22:6). Ahab asked if he should go or refrain, and the answer was go. Not one voice picked the couch.

No waiting is mentioned. The prophets say, “Go up,” and “…the Lord will deliver it into the hand of the king.” (1 Kings 22:6). Ahab asked go or refrain, and they answered go. In this verse, nobody asks for more time or a bigger army.

Yes. Ahab says Micaiah “…never prophesies anything good for me, but only bad.” (1 Kings 22:8). The reason he gives is the kind of news Micaiah brings. That's like being mad at the oven timer for going off.

Ahab never says Micaiah is untrue. His complaint is that Micaiah “…never prophesies anything good for me, but only bad.” (1 Kings 22:8). The reason he gives is the kind of news, good or bad. Truth doesn't come up in what he says.

Yes. Zedekiah, son of Chenaanah, says the LORD declares, “With these you shall gore the Arameans until they are finished off.” (1 Kings 22:11). The king of Aram is the one Ahab says he hasn't taken Ramoth-gilead from. Zedekiah brings a prop for the point he's making.

Philistines aren't in this scene. Zedekiah, son of Chenaanah, says, “With these you shall gore the Arameans until they are finished off.” (1 Kings 22:11). The Arameans are the people of the king Ahab says he hasn't taken the city from. Zedekiah's iron horns come with a message about Aram.

Yes. The messenger tells Micaiah, “Behold now, with one accord the words of the prophets are favorable to the king. So please let your words be like theirs, and speak favorably.” (1 Kings 22:13). He's asking Micaiah to match the other prophets. That's a lot of pressure to put on one man.

The messenger doesn't ask for silence. He says, “So please let your words be like theirs, and speak favorably.” (1 Kings 22:13). He wants Micaiah to speak, and to sound like the other prophets. He's asking Micaiah to sing along, not sit the song out.

The LORD doesn't mention prophets there. He says, “These people have no master; let each one return home in peace.” (1 Kings 22:17). The word is master, like the shepherd in the picture. Funny enough, prophets are all over this scene.
Yes. Ahab says to Jehoshaphat, “Did I not tell you that he never prophesies good for me, but only bad?” (1 Kings 22:18). He's counting it as proof. He turns to Jehoshaphat like the case is closed.

The spirit doesn't say soldiers. He says, “I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.” (1 Kings 22:22). The mouths in question belong to the prophets. Soldiers aren't named in that line.

Yes, friend. Micaiah answers Zedekiah, “You will soon see, on that day when you go and hide in an inner room.” (1 Kings 22:25). Zedekiah had just struck him in the face, and this is his answer. He doesn't say what that day will look like, and I won't guess.

Micaiah doesn't mention Ramoth-gilead in his answer. He says, “You will soon see, on that day when you go and hide in an inner room.” (1 Kings 22:25). The day he points to is about Zedekiah hiding. Zedekiah had just struck him in the face, and that's the answer he gives.

The king does send Micaiah away next, but that's not the day Micaiah names. He says, “You will soon see, on that day when you go and hide in an inner room.” (1 Kings 22:25). Micaiah is talking about what Zedekiah will do. Zedekiah had struck him in the face, and this is the word he gives back.

Yes. Ahab says, “Put this man in prison and feed him only bread and water until I return safely.” (1 Kings 22:27). Ahab's order has an end date in it, and it's his own safe return. The order also says to feed Micaiah only bread and water.

There's no gate duty in Ahab's order. He says, “Put this man in prison and feed him only bread and water until I return safely.” (1 Kings 22:27). Ahab orders prison, and he names his own safe return as the end of it. A guard at the gate would've been a much nicer spot.

Yes. Micaiah says, “If you ever return safely, the LORD has not spoken through me.” (1 Kings 22:28). He says it right after the king orders him to prison. He puts the whole test on one thing: whether Ahab returns safely.
